Sheminith
SHEM-ih-nith
noun
Hebrew shemīnīth, “the eighth,” from shemōneh, “eight”; understood as the octave below, the lower or bass register, or an eight-stringed instrument; set over against Alamoth, the higher voices.

📖 Biblical Definition

Sheminith, “the eighth,” heads the sixth and the twelfth psalms, and is named in the order of David’s singers, where certain Levites played “with harps on the Sheminith to excel” (1Ch 15:21). It is most received as denoting the lower register — the octave beneath, the grave bass of the men’s voices and the deeper strings — set in deliberate contrast to Alamoth, the maidens’ or higher part (1Ch 15:20). The sixth psalm, sung upon Sheminith, is the first of the seven penitential psalms: “O LORD, rebuke me not in thine anger, neither chasten me in thy hot displeasure” (Psa 6:1), and the deep notes well befit so grave a cry. The twelfth likewise mourns the failing of the faithful from among men. Here is a quiet wisdom: the very registers of the congregation’s song were ordered under God, the high and the low, the maiden and the man, each given a part, that the whole assembly might lift a full and tempered praise. The body of Christ is no monotone. As in the temple choir the deep voices answered the high, so in the church the strong and the weak, the glad and the grieving, blend their distinct notes into one harmony before the throne.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

The eighth, or the lower octave; the bass register of the temple song, set over against the higher Alamoth.

SHEMINITH, a Hebrew word signifying “the eighth,” from the number eight.

It is most received as denoting the octave below, the bass or lower register of voices and strings.

It heads the sixth and twelfth psalms and is named in the order of David’s singers.

It is set in contrast to Alamoth, the higher or maidens’ part.

It witnesses that the very registers of the congregation’s praise were ordered under God.

📖 Key Scripture

Psa 6, title — "To the chief Musician on Neginoth upon Sheminith, A Psalm of David."

Psa 12, title — "To the chief Musician upon Sheminith, A Psalm of David."

1Ch 15:21 — "And Mattithiah, and Elipheleh, and Mikneiah, and Obededom, and Jeiel, and Azaziah, with harps on the Sheminith to excel."

Psa 6:1 — "O LORD, rebuke me not in thine anger, neither chasten me in thy hot displeasure."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

A direction of register, not a contested doctrine; it pictures the ordered harmony of the whole congregation, the deep voices answering the high before the throne.

expand to see more

Sheminith names the lower register of the temple song and faces no postmodern redefinition. The truth it pictures, however, stands against both a flattening uniformity and a chaos of self-expression in worship: the body of Christ is neither a monotone nor a babel, but a tempered harmony in which every appointed part has its place.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the ordered fulness of congregational praise. As the deep voices upon Sheminith answered the high voices upon Alamoth, so in the church the strong and the weak, the rejoicing and the penitent, lift their distinct notes into one harmony. None is left out, and none is left to himself; all are gathered under the rule of the word into a single song to God.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

From the Hebrew for “the eighth,” Sheminith names the lower octave of the temple song, the deep voices answering the high in ordered praise.

expand to see more

Sheminith — Hebrew shemīnīth, “the eighth,” from shemōneh, eight.

It denotes the octave below, the bass or lower register.

It heads the sixth and twelfth psalms, both grave in their burden.

Levites played “with harps on the Sheminith to excel” (1Ch 15:21).

It is set over against Alamoth, the higher or maidens’ part.

Usage

"The deep notes of Sheminith befit the penitential cry of the sixth psalm."

"As the low voices answered the high, the whole congregation lifted a full and tempered praise."

"The body of Christ is no monotone: strong and weak, glad and grieving, blend into one harmony."
